description:
The first public hall places an unexplained sabre beside coastal objects with ordinary uses: a bell, sounding weights, a shipping ledger and ceramics. The attendant distinguishes evidence from conjecture. Seeing the blade is a visit, not acquiring it.

Proposed curatorial practice: labels distinguish an object’s reported find-place from what wear and material actually show. A cracked sounding weight can be useful evidence without being valuable treasure; an incomplete shipping ledger can identify a trade route without explaining a drowned people. Later, the player can bring a rubbing or a careful description from a submerged threshold and compare it with an ordinary collection piece. Similarity supports a question; it does not certify the sabre’s maker or a full account of the catastrophe. The missing blade leaves an empty mounting and an interrupted ordinary display, not a newly revealed altar.

data.description: Proposed comparison of ordinary coastal objects and late underwater finds. Museum knowledge is partial; the comparison does not settle the sabre’s origin.
